items.label: July 1945
items.sum: News of members: the death of sprinter Alec Mewes, members held as prisoners of war, news of members serving in the Forces at home and overseas, and notes on members and old members at home.
items.s: NEWS OF MEMBERS News of members: the death of sprinter Alec Mewes, members held as prisoners of war, news of members serving in the Forces at home and overseas, and notes on members and old members at home. We announce with deepest regret the following death:— Alec Mewes was killed in France. He was 29 years old and joined us in 1928 when only 13 years old. He was one of our best known sprinters in pre-war days, and figured in many relay teams. He was also a useful long jumper and had represented us on countless occasions in Club matches. He was a keen athlete, modest and popular. Our deepest sympathies are extended to his widow. Prisoners of War Les Bennett. We learn from Mrs. Bennett that no news has been received from Les for well over a year, when a brief message stated that he was fit and well in Java. Our sympathies are extended to Olive and we all sincerely trust that Les is well and hope for a speedy return. Dan and Alec Patience. Last heard of in Stalag XIA (between Magdeburg and Berlin. We hear from brother Ron that they are fit and well but, unfortunately, have little facilities for exercise. Alf Miller and Arthur Beales were at Stalagluft III at Sagan and were both in good health. Frank Halls was at Stalag 344 at Lansdorf, and his latest news was that his leg was making progress and that he was in good health. * * * * The daily papers have kept us informed of how the occupants of these camps were marched 400 miles across Germany. With the Allies' occupation of Germany, the liberation of our five members should soon be announced. We hope that we shall soon be welcoming their return. * * * * Alf Harley was recently promoted to Squadron Leader. Congratulations, Alf! It can now be revealed that he is stationed at Caserta. He has been getting some of the R.A.F. fellows out running (no, Alf did not run himself). He has met two old athletic friends in Squire Yarrow (Poly.) and Ron Pantling (London Vidarians). Like many others, his experience of Italian rain and snow has caused him to have decided views on "Sunny Italy." Bert Footer visited the Hall early in the year whilst on embarkation leave. He hinted something about Burma and the East. Bert had a spin with Tom Carter and Co. and showed that being a Commando has definitely not affected his running. Bert carries our best wishes wherever he is and we trust that he will return soon. Bill Sutton denies the rumour that he had gained the Military Medal; in fact, he's far behind the lines! He is still in Corsica, and recommends it as ideal walking and climbing country. Little scope for athletics. Frank Elson, after his strenuous time with the R.E.M.E., had a spell in hospital for shock, but is now better again—in fact, he looked in at the Hall a short time ago and looked bronzed and very fit. Jack Shotter. The latest news is that he is now in the fighting in Burma. Len Coleman. His recent accident, we now learn, was a plane crash. He has been in hospital again to be "sliced open," and is now taking things easy. He is stationed near another member, Jim Hewitt. Charlie Churcher is still awaiting the boat home. Is unable to do any training—even a few strolls. Had an enjoyable Christmas, food, beer, football matches and concerts, but he would rather do a Godstone and back walk. Norman Graves has, by his running exploits, won a warm place in the hearts of the French people. He has turned out with the local club and performed creditably. He has won prizes and medals to bring home. He competed in an important race round the famous Bois de Boulogne (Paris). In another race, against French cracks, he was third, only few yards behind the winner. Dick Towndrow has been training regularly and nearly broke a leg at football. He had a narrow escape on Christmas Day when he was in a building which collapsed. We gave him an extra stripe in the last mag.. he is a Lance Corporal. Colin Sutton, has been regraded and may be coming home. Is still fit, as he was second in a 5,000 metres walk at the Bengal Olympic Games on February 8th. The winner was N. K. Das, time 27mins. 40.4secs. Bill Snell has been transferred from A.A. to R.A.S.C. He narrowly missed seeing Charlie Churcher recently. He is now in Syria where there is plenty of ski-ing over the mountains, so we can guess he's pretty fit. George Durrant is now in Burma where he complains of the heat and flies. In spite of constant sweating he is "as fat as a pig." Is hoping for 28 days "Blighty" leave. Jimmy Kemp is still wandering the globe, last heard of in Somaliland. Dick Stride has recovered from his wounds which he got in Italy, and has since been twice mentioned in dispatches. Eric Keyworth met Len Spooner in Jerusalem and succeeded him as Sports Officer. Has collected 3 Palestine Championship Medals with relay teams. Has had moderate success in road races. Percy Wilson found pictures, etc., of the 1936 Olympic Games when searching a house in Germany. Reuben Bradshaw is now with the Welsh Guards in the B.L.A., and was very pleased to receive the Club Christmas Card. "Stimmo" has been doing some running over the other side with the B.L.A. In a recent letter he expresses his gratitude for the advice and encouragement given to him in his junior days by Dick Savage. Len Marchant still sends cheery letters from the Azores. He has contacted Ray Dunford who is also in those parts. Will Rispin sends us greetings from the front line with the B.L.A. Len Fletcher aroused the interest of the locals when he went for a spin on a track in Holland. We regret to learn from Len that his father died recently. Mr. Fletcher was a staunch supporter at walking events, and was full of encouragement for Len and Jack. Our sympathies to both Len and Jack on their loss. Charlie Smart is still with the B.L.A., and manages to do a bit of running with a few French athletes. Teddy Read is now a Fying Officer attached to the 14th Army; he is grounded for a time but is quite happy. This we learn from Lilian, who also informs us that Norman Shrubb is also a Flying Officer, and is also Sports Officer covering almost every branch of sport. Is working very hard. Frank Webb writes from Port Alfred, South Africa, to say that at last he has done some running. In a one mile race he was third in 4.43, and third in the half mile in 2.8. Frank found the going a bit hard after a two years' absence from running. He has been keeping fit by swimming. Joe Edwards hasn't been doing any running lately as he's been spending most of his time in the sun on top of a telegraph pole in the desert in Tripoli. He is now in an office and has played a little football and hockey to keep his waistline in order. Tony Bellchambers, with S.E.A.C., has had a short spell in hospital with malaria, but is now fit again. Francis is still with East African Command. Arthur Beaumont has been rushing about in Italy but is as right as rain. Speaks in glowing terms of the welcome they get in the villages and the Italian girls. Longs for a sight of Battersea Park. Etienne Gailley, who was whisked from our last issue to his native Belgium, visited us early in the year in the uniform of an "umbrella man." He was pleased to tell us that he had met his family again. He was also pleased to come back and see his running friends in England. Ken Webb, who joined the R.A.F. and went to Canada and collected three stripes, is, we understand, back in England, doing his stuff! Max Quackenbos must be feeling dizzy after the Indoor Season, running on a board track eleven laps to the mile. In the A.A.U. 3 Miles, he was 8th. At the Millrose Games he was 3rd in a Two Miles Handicap, off 75 yards. He was a close 4th in the Billings 2 Miles, won in 9-19-6, and 7th in the Toussaint Two Miles (New York A.C.), won in 9-17-6. "Quack" still sends us programmes profusely illustrated, which outclass most of our pre-war programmes. What would our American friends say to one of our wartime typewritten affairs with no photographs, no advertisements, and little space for scribbling in results and lap times (when given!)? Jack Fletcher sends us a long and interesting letter from India. Beginning with reminiscences of running and socials, he then reviews his career in the Services. After two years in the R.A.P.C., "Nobby" went through various courses, and finally found his way out to India with an Infantry Brigade. Cyril Pateman writes from Ceylon to say that it will not be long before he is back at the Hall where he hopes to be of assistance to us. Len Herbert has made several appearances this winter as he has been stationed not very far from the Hall. His brother, Eric, paid us a leave and by now is probably over the water. Percy Wright has recently been to Preston on an Army Education Course and may soon be blossoming forth as an Army teacher. The good work with the B.N.L. continues, including a personal letter to ALL overseas walkers. Just think of it, nearly 50 issues of the B.N.L. have appeared; with ten or a dozen walkers overseas, that means that he must have written some 500 letters! Percy still pays occasional visits to town for a race, and, of course, if there's any walking in S. Wales, he's in it. Recently he forwarded £2 10s. to the Hon. Treasurer, the proceeds from the sale of airgraphs. Money raised in this manner is earmarked for an "Overseas Cup" for the walkers. Incidentally, B.N.L. stands for Belgrave News Letter. Jack Rutland is still at Manorbier, S. Wales. His training on Welsh roads has kept him in fine form—see walking results. He made a first-class effort in the Club Open to secure an Individual win for the Club, but was beaten into second place by a few yards. Charlie Redgrave was recently "on the air" in "Merry-Go-Round," when he gave a turn similar to those he used to give at Club socials, a song with his banjo, interspersed with some tap-dancing. Charlie has a pretty busy time entertaining and arranging concerts for the Forces. Gave his shoes an airing to help the Club to win the wartime Surrey County Road-Walking title. Charlie, who is stationed in Lincs, visits our Brighton walker, C. A. Wattam. Bill Jones recently married a V.A.D. attached to his unit at Leeds. Congratulations and best wishes to you both. He hasn't done any racing recently although there's not much scope for winter walking in those parts. Jimmy Green has been resting his leg after he was "spiked." Is busy planning his big meeting at Gillingham, June 23rd. Don't forget the date! Arthur Cook, our megaphone man, has moved from Dorset to Aldershot, which town he couples with "Blanco" and "Spit and Polish." Is hoping to come along and see us at track meetings. His wife presented him with twin girls last November. Double congratulations! George Murray visited the Hall after five years absence to have a run with the boys before going over the water. Ken Cuff was able to pay us a few visits when stationed near London. He is now up in Scotland with the Black Watch. Doug. Woodhead has been temporarily grounded and has done little running lately. Bill True is still busy at Sandhurst, but was able to visit us and turn out at the Open Walk. Laurie Jackson is still undergoing treatment and is having a skin grafting at the back of his knee. He is now at St. Albans. Will Applebee, as a member of the "Silent Service," doesn't say much except that he has been about a good bit, but has managed to get a few leaves. Harry Churcher celebrated Boxing Day with a stroll from Manston to Deal. Is very busy at his station and is hoping that their efforts will help to shorten the war so that he can get home and back to the form which made him A.A.A. Champion at 2 and 7 miles, etc. George Cockburn is up North, training for a Navigator Wireless Operator. At recent Service Sports he returned 10.2secs. for the 100, 23secs. for the 220 and 4.31 for the mile. Len Camin writes that he is very busy with the R.A.S.C. in Gloucestershire. Wally Ives arrived home to "Blighty" after some time in India, just in time to see the Open Walk. Although he has spent some time "in dock," he was looking very fit and was obviously pleased to be with us again. He will probably soon be demobbed and back on the trolleybuses again. We congratulate him on becoming a Sergeant. With him at the Hall were his two boys, who are members. Ernest Reeve, one of our walkers of bygone years, from Chelmsford, went to France, came back via Dunkirk, and is now in Shropshire with the R.E.M.E. Bert Smith is with the A.C.C. in the Shetlands and has been busy on the "grub-stakes." Paid a visit to the Hall, accompanied by his small son, during March. Len Spooner managed an appointment with Percy Wright in a pub at Newport. Has turned out for us in a few "Opens." Bert Clayton, home from Aden and sent to Wales where he, too, met Percy. When he visited his home town, Eastleigh, he had a few spins with Tommy Green. P. C. Bannister is now back from I.o.M., and it is rumoured that he led the way home in walks. Stan Botwright always seems to be on the move, his latest address being Norfolk. Joe Coleman still very busy, but paid us a visit and had a spin in the L.F.F. Open Walk. Joe was obviously short of training, but gave us a chance to see the style which has won him prizes for both speed and style. John Brown, our Southern Junior Half-Mile Champion, has been called away at a most interesting period of his running career and is now at Scarborough. Derek Pollard is another youngster called to the services just when he had hoped to put in some good running. Derek was posted to the Guards Depot at Caterham. We learn from his father that he is in the Grenadiers, likes the life and is now a fine, strapping youth. Doug. Earle, who used to race in the days of Len Fletcher and Don Brown, for they all worked at the same firm, is now in the R.A.F., stationed at Tangmere. We also learn that he is married. Jack Field has been with an A.A. battery on the E. Coast. Took part in a services' road walk to find himself up against Tom Richardson, the Woodford Green Record Holder! Jack is anxious to trace a medal he passed on to the Club for engraving before the war. It is a winning team medal for the Surrey County Road Walk Championship, 1938. Can anyone give any information, please? Tommy Scrimshaw paid us a welcome visit before going over the water. Ernie Duffett, in spite of the flying bomb incident, reported in the last issue, still resides in and helps law and order in Croydon. He has other pressing calls, but he still knows enough about us to be our Hon. Handicapper—a fact regretfully omitted from the list of officers in the last mag. Charlie Cook is now back in the S.W.11 district again after being bombed out. The bomb had a bad effect on his hearing and we all sympathise with him. But Charlie manages; he is undoubtedly our best recruiting agent, as a good proportion of our new members have been introduced to us by him. He is one of the "regulars" at the track. Nice work, and thank you, Charlie. Frank Thomson has been much better this winter and has lent a hand at Club fixtures. He is also continuing the work behind the scenes with the A.A.A. Bill Fish sends his heartfelt thanks to Club members for their kindness and sympathy during his recent illness. We are pleased to say that Bill is much better and we hope that he will enjoy watching many, many track meetings with us. George Still has been one of the regulars at the Hall. George obviously doesn't mind the weather as he turned up on Boxing Day (remember how cold it was?) and gained second prize in the two miles run. Jack Carne and father again send us good wishes from Worthing, particularly to their old Club friends. Ken O' Kell has left Manchester and is now back in town (Chingford). I wonder what he thinks of doodle-bugs! Stan Blunden writes from Kidderminster to say that he had a fairly good track season last year. Is hoping to see the lads when they are competing in the Midlands. He reports that their baby is progressing well. Reg. Johnson sends a Club vest and badge from Stockport. Has done no running himself lately, but hopes that his two sons will do some C.-C. running in a few years. "P. J." Gorner hopes to be busy on the track after resting his foot. Bill Ashford, who went to Iran some years ago, turned up at the Club early in the year. After a leave at home he was due to return to Iran. Many will remember Bill running on track and country before the war, but in Iran things are different and he's had no running out there. John Rowland never fails to visit us when on vacation from his medical studies at Aberdeen, where he has revived interest in running amongst his fellow students. George Tyrer has been unable to visit us as he has been working seven days a week. Perhaps we will be seeing him next season. Oscar Horwood, we are sorry to say, has had a bad bout of sciatica and we trust that the fine weather will see him out and well again. How many know of the debt the Club owes to Oscar? After the last war the Club's fortunes were at a very low ebb and it was entirely due to the persistence and enthusiasm of a small band, of which Oscar was a prominent worker, that the Club survived. Oscar's efforts have been amply rewarded and when he sees the Club's present position, his thoughts go back to those days. He was honoured by being elected Club President two or three years before this war. Jack Bidgood is very busy as S.D.I. at a Police Station in S. London (no, it's nothing to do with Soft Drinks Industry!) Is hoping to put his racing shoes on again after the war. Len Box was a recent visitor to the Hall, and is now living on the S. Coast. Len Storey is another old 'un to visit us recently. How about bringing your togs next time, Len? Wally Bayliss, complete in brown corduroys, turned up at the Hall straight from his "farm" at Woking with a real chicken's egg for old Harry Parker. He hopes (?) to visit us more frequently. Sid King, another "old 'un," complete with R.W.A. Gold Medal and push bike, was an onlooker (shame!) at the Open Walk. Frank Thorn, although in the forties, polished his shoes and raced in both the Open and County Walks. His feet gave him trouble and although he put up a good performance in the Open, he had to retire from the County Race. Harry Stanford, who displayed so much enthusiam this winter season, was unlucky when he started track training at Tooting. He broke a small bone in his foot which necessitated his foot being put into plaster and the use of an iron. We trust that there is no permanent damage. John Weames, anoher of Fred Ford's, insisted on turning out for the Club in the National Youths' C.-C. Race in spite of a bad cold. He ran a plucky race and finished 73rd. Reg. Elson has been seen watching road walks. Here's another we hope to see in the Club's teams again. Syd Roberts hasn't been very active this season as he had a bad bout of influenza. He has, however, captained the walkers again to good effect. We all trust that Syd will soon get fit and back to form. Jimmy Flatt is still very busy and out in all weathers, which has made him a bit "chesty," but Jimmy carries on! Fred Ford nowadays concentrates his energies on finding us promising youngsters, one of which is a National (Junior) Champion. A rather high standard to keep up, but leave it to Fred! Ted Jackman hopes to be on the road again after having had treatment for foot trouble. Bert Lindsey is another who works long and inconvenient hours, but he occasionally manages a run from the Hall. David Main has our sympathies on having had his home badly damaged by a rocket. George McKeown, our North Country member, keeps fit during the winter as wing three-quarter with the Rosslyn Park Rugger Pack. His prowess at the game got him a place in a Civil Defence XV. Nice work, George! Ben May, whose six foot odd of height and umpteen stones weight earned him the nickname of "Big Ben," has been running with Bournemouth A.C. Harry Verney was soon found a job when he visited us, and he looked as if he was enjoying the sound of shoes on mud again. Syd Warboys has moved from Essex to Wallasey, Cheshire. Mick Walker is now convalescing from an attack of pleurisy. We all hope that Mick will soon be well again. Tommy Moore, of Belvedere, who joined in 1920 and was one of that famous school of veteran sprinters from North Kent which in their heyday used to give handicappers such headaches, sends his regards to all his "old cronies." Harold King, of Bob Ricketts' day, has, with the revival of athletics in North Kent, been out doing a spot of judging. Another is Warren. H. F. Jacques and W. T. Luther, also of this school, have promised help. Joe Turner, our "Grade A" Timekeeper, is, we are pleased to learn, recovering from the nasty accident he met with in mid-winter—"when the snow lay round about." When alighting from a train when on his way to a cross-country run, he slipped and one leg went between the platform and the train. His presence of mind in throwing himself to the ground avoided what might have been a very serious affair. items.s: RUNNING RESULTS — SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C.A. Belgrave results in the Southern Counties C.C.A.'s five team races of 1944–45 (Belgrave Hall, Hayes, Ruislip, Belgrave Hall and Epsom); the Epsom report gives Belgrave an easy team win with 28 points to Poly.'s 45 but the printed team result is 1st Poly. 42, 2nd Belgrave 61. Once again this Association promoted 5 team races, the first at Belgrave Hall on October 14th. A first class entry of fifteen teams had been made for this, the first of the series of five races promoted by this Association. Owing to the starting field being mainly occupied as a "battle course," the course was under five miles. Three teams had been entered from the Club and 29 members finished. Tom Carter and Gosney (Eastleigh) soon sorted themselves out, followed by George Hoath and took the field along at a rare pace and these places were maintained to the finish, although Tom made a game effort. The chief feature of the race was the forward running of several of the younger school, particularly Stan Eeles who perhaps ran his best race to date—Stan has the makings of a real runner if he will get down to it, Fred Clay, John Brown, Bob Boyden, Norman Walker and Alf Heathfield. The "A" team were beaten by Eastleigh for first place with a 19 points margin. Result: 1 R. Lucas third. Herbert, L. W. (4), Cohen (10) and Pearson (13) gave the Bels an easy victory in the team race with 28 pts. from Poly. (45). 1st, Poly., 42 points; 2nd, Belgrave, 61 points. All of the winning team deserve special mention, for George Lucas (now a proud father) is unable to train with us as much as he would like; Len Herbert also without serious training, ran his best race of the season. Les Cohen, with worries no end and only a fortnight's training, proved that he can still beat Harry Shields into the winning team. items.label: July 1945
items.sum: Harry Verney's report of the first National Youths' Race, won by Belgrave's Burfitt, and the District Associations' Team Race won by the South, at Dartmouth Park, West Bromwich, on March 10th, 1945.
items.s: A DAY AT THE RACES Harry Verney's report of the first National Youths' Race, won by Belgrave's Burfitt, and the District Associations' Team Race won by the South, at Dartmouth Park, West Bromwich, on March 10th, 1945. Saturday, March 10th, 1945, has proved to be one day in these war-torn years that can remain a very happy memory for the South and, in particular, for the "Bels.," for on that day was decided the first National Youths' Race and the District Associations' Team Race in Dartmouth Park, West Bromwich. The weather was extremely fine, but perhaps a shade too warm for a fast, seven miles cross country race, and the ground conditions were firm; in fact, spikes or rubbers could have been worn with no decided advantage over either choice. The Youths' Race which preceded the District Race attracted 17 teams and 10 individuals—101 runners started—and comprised two laps of parkland, each lap measuring a distance of 1½ miles. From the fall of the starting flag the race was dominated by our own Burfitt. At the end of the first lap he was comfortably ahead by some 90 yards and the farther he went the greater the lead he gained. Full of running, he finished some 250 yards in front of Farrell, of Hallamshire, with Rouse, of South London Harriers, third, 65 yards behind Farrell. It was bad luck for the Northern youth that he came up against a runner of Burfitt's calibre, for Farrell himself is outstanding and I predict in him a future northern champion at least, but Burfitt, of course, was super, as Farrell was only too ready to agree. Unfortunately, only three Belgrave runners turned up at Paddington and so we were prevented from starting with even a scoring team and the depleted team were made to run as individuals. The winning team was Barry Boys' Council School with 47 points—a grand team. Burfitt's time was 16mins. 58.2secs.; Farrell's, 17mins. 36secs.; and Rouse's, 17mins. 52 secs. So to the Senior Race. This comprised four laps of the course covered by the youths plus an additional ¼ mile detour on each lap. The end of the first lap saw Gosney, Hughes and Bunton running together in a bunch, with our "evergreen" Tom Carter in close attendance. Behind Tom came Reid, of Birchfield and Scottish International, to be followed by Cole, of Dudley, the Junior International. Bingham was about ten yards behind Cole and close to him followed two Northern men, Ellis and Tyrer. The second lap saw no change in the leading positions, but Reid had jumped ahead of Carter, who was running on his own some 15 yards from the Birchfielder. Bingham trailed Carter, and a few yards behind Bingham came Hoath, who on this lap had moved up to 7th from 13th position. Jack Holden, the oft-times International, was 9th. The pace continued hot. The end of the third lap saw no change in the first seven positions. Tom was still running in his own solitary company and appeared to be finding things a bit tough as he passed me, though he was running as determined as ever. It was obvious at this stage that the South were going to swamp the other districts and if the Midlands and North combined teams, the South would still win hands down. The race finished up an incline of 600 yards, some 400 yards of it gruellingly steep, and it was for this finish that Hughes had been waiting to jump Gosney, who has no love for hills, a fact Hughes knew. So the Poly. man ran out the winner by some 35 yards in 37 mins. 2 secs. Gosney (37mins. 10secs.) easily held off Reid (37mins. 17secs.), who in turn held off Bunton (37mins. 31secs.). Tom came racing in very strongly to finish 5th (37mins. 36secs.). Not only had he got over any distress he was experiencing on the start of the final lap, but he was running more strongly than any of the men who had finished ahead of him, and he was moving up fast on Bunton. Incidentally, I consider that Bunton ran the wrong type of race. Instead of hanging on with Gosney and Hughes he should have gone to the front and forced the pace after the second lap. Still, experience will come with the years ahead. Hoath moved up on this lap to take Bingham's place in 6th position (37mins. 46secs.), while the Finchley man lost 7th place to Ferguson, of Birchfield, with Holden behind Bingham in 9th place. Thus did the South "rise and shine" to place six men in the first eight positions. It was Herbert's distinct misfortune to experience a real off-day, not only in the running sense, but physically, too, for as he passed me on every lap he showed unmistakable signs of distress and it must have been sheer "guts" and will-power that enabled him to complete the course. I understand that the team, on arrival back at Paddington, ran a "dead heat" to the nearest pub and wallowed in war-time "wobble" on a lend-lease basis until closing time. Team result—South, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8: 26 points; Midlands, 3, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13: 53 points; North, 12, 16, 18, 20, 21, 25: 112 points. HARRY VERNEY. items.sum: A. W. Jannaway urges Belgrave juniors to train regularly at Wimbledon, since the post-war teams must be built from them, and asks them to send him their preferred distances.
items.s: JUNIOR NOTES A. W. Jannaway urges Belgrave juniors to train regularly at Wimbledon, since the post-war teams must be built from them, and asks them to send him their preferred distances. Juniors would do well to remember that it is from their ranks that the post-war teams must be built up. Belgrave Harriers have been represented in big events for a decade or more by a combination of runners probably unprecedented in the history of athletics. It is difficult to realise that we are now in the sixth winter season since he war began and many of our established champions and others are slowly but inevitably approaching the veteran stage. The future reputation and good name of the Club is therefore in the hands of the seniors of tomorrow. Whether the name of Belgrave will mean so much in five years' time as it does now depends on the basis of sound training put in by the juniors of today. Regular training in mid-week is advisable, but regular training at Wimbledon is essential, for the art of running can only by learnt from experience with better men, and the necessary grit for strenuous work is best acquired by running in company. Information of any kind on training will gladly be given by senior members. The undersigned would also like those juniors who really mean business to let him know what distances they fancy, with indication of performances. Finally, don't forget to fetch along any pal who is interested and shows ability. That's the way the Club was built up. A. W. JANNAWAY. 137 Craddocks Avenue, Ashstead, Surrey. A. W. Jannaway A. W. JANNAWAY wrote Junior Notes; 137 Craddocks Avenue, Ashstead, Surrey Wimbledon Ashstead Surrey Belgrave Harriers

items.label: July 1945
items.sum: Review of the Belgrave walkers' sixth war-time winter season, recalling pre-war successes, with the result of the Club Open Walk won by W. L. Burgess from Jack Rutland.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS Review of the Belgrave walkers' sixth war-time winter season, recalling pre-war successes, with the result of the Club Open Walk won by W. L. Burgess from Jack Rutland. As we come to the close of our sixth, and we hope, last war-time winter season, we can look back with a high degree of satisfaction at having been able to keep the Belgrave colours so much to the fore during such difficult times. During the years immediately preceding the war, it was quite a common occurrence for us to finish anything up to half a dozen in the first ten in Open "Sevens" and on one occasion in the Ashcombe Open we actually took the first six places. Other pre-war successes included 1938 and 1939 winners of both Junior and National 20 Championships, 1937 and 1938, Harry Churcher first home in every open seven. 1938, Colin Sutton's hat-trick in being placed in the winning teams in the Junior, National and 50 Kilos; 1938, Joe and Len Coleman dead heating for first place in the Junior. What grand memories to look back on! Then came the war and our star walkers gradually trickled away to the various services, and so to all parts of the world, leaving mainly our police members to carry on. As time went on they too gradually disappeared. Norman Dyne, Frank Halls and others. As far as conditions would permit, our Service members came from all parts of the country to help build up the teams. Percy Wright, Jack Rutland, Charlie Redgrave, Bill Jones, and many others. We naturally haven't been able to secure many youngsters as they, too, have been absorbed into the Services just when they would normally have started racing and so we have had to fall back on men beyond the calling up age and their best racing years, but nevertheless keen enough to turn out week after week and thus ensure that even if the Club colours couldn't always be so conspicuous amongst the leaders, it would be evident to the walking world and our absent Club mates they didn't intend to let the Club lie dormant during the war period. Without their assistance we should certainly have been hard pushed to find teams on several occasions and our gratitude goes out to them for their invaluable assistance. We have, however, been able to secure two promising juniors in A. Joels and J. Scamell, the latter being introduced by his father, an old Club member. Both have been giving a good account of themselves during the past season. With these two and young Mac, we have the foundations of a good post-war junior team. Jack Rutland and Percy Wright, who have for so long been trying to get the Army Athletic Board to give road walking its proper place in Army athletics, have at last met with a measure of success, insomuch as they were selected to represent the Army in the 15 and 20 miles opens. We hope there will be more to follow and that this is only a small beginning to bigger things. Amongst the most noteworthy Club performances during the season are those of Jack Rutland, second to Whitlock in the Woodford Green Open and again second to Burgess in our own open. Eddie Jury, our Portsmouth member, has been first home on three occasions, each time beating Alexander, of Portsmouth City Police. Bob McMullen found his best form in the B.W.S.A. Open when he finished third The season opened by us tying with Surrey W.C. for scratch team honours. In December, at Wimbledon, we brought off a double in the Surrey "Boxing Day" Five, being first in both scratch and handicap team races. In our own open we had first place in both team and individual handicaps and second in team and individual scratch races. Bob Readman and Harry Rouse finished second and third respectively in the Police Ten and the following Saturday we met with success in the Surrey County Race, R. McMullen and H. Rouse finishing second and third respectively and the Club taking team honours. The same day A. Joels finished third in the Kent race. With Eddie Jury in London, we took second team place in the scratch race and a similar placing in the handicap section of the B.W.S.A. Open. Altogether a very creditable season's work. May we look forward to just as successful a summer season and hope that by the time the next road season comes round we shall have some of our Services men back with us, until then we can rest assured that everyone will do their best to give the Club a good show. The Club Open Walk was again a big reunion for our walkers past and present. The new three-lap course was used, which gave spectators several chances to see the race and urge on their clubmates. The entry of some ninety-odd was well up to the war-time average and many famous walkers took part. The race for individual honours was a close thing and Jack Rutland failed by a few seconds. Nevertheless, congratulations came to Jack from everybody for his great performance, which must also be judged from the fact that he had made a long journey from Pembrokeshire and that he does not get the necessary competition for a front ranker. We were pleased to receive entries from Godiva Harriers, Coventry. Although the race is not run for profit, our Walking Secretary, Syd. Roberts, was able to show a small balance. We thank Syd. and the many Club folk who turned up and helped to make the event a success. The Club is greatly indebted to Jimmy Bellchambers, Harry Evans, Wally Ives and Syd. items.sum: Three-month training schedule for milers compiled from A. R. Shaw's diary, with an introduction on Albert Shaw's pre-war running and his foreword of training advice.
items.s: A SCHEDULE FOR MILERS AND TWO-MILERS COMPILED FROM A. R. SHAW'S DIARY Three-month training schedule for milers compiled from A. R. Shaw's diary, with an introduction on Albert Shaw's pre-war running and his foreword of training advice. Introduction Older members need no introduction to Albert Shaw, but for others it will be of interest to be reminded that just prior to the war, Albert was one of our most consistent milers. He was several times runner-up in our Club Championships, consistently beat 4.30secs. and was in many winning two-mile team races. Apart from this he won many opens and was placed in several Business House Championships. Anyone knowing Albert will appreciate the thought and energy he put into his running and I'm sure that the table will be of interest and use to members. If the table does no more than encourage the study and reading of the various books on athletics which can be obtained from the library, it is well justified. Foreword by A. R. Shaw I take pleasure in submitting the following schedule on how to prepare yourself for a mile. It is considered that, starting in April, it will take three months to reach your peak performances. It is assumed that you have had a season on the country to strengthen your body, so that what is now required is steady building up for speed. Miling today is a fast business. All work must, so far as possible, be to a stop-watch. Be well and warmly clothed and do ample warming up before starting your run. Keep good hours and regular habits. Eat good food and plenty of honey, barley sugar, etc. Obtain by experiment your best racing weight and when it drops below normal, rest for a few days. Work Club races in with your training, but do not race your distance in mid-week matches. SCHEDULE V.S. denotes varying strides. items.label: November 1945
items.sum: Editorial welcoming demobilised members, announcing a return to the full pre-war programme and recalling the club's pre-war titles and individual champions.
e: R.W.A. National Junior Ten Miles Championship
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial welcoming demobilised members, announcing a return to the full pre-war programme and recalling the club's pre-war titles and individual champions. Since the last issue events have moved quickly. The sudden ending of hostilities in the Far East has brought Peace to the World again. A number of our members have already been demobilised and many others hope to return to civilian life soon. We extend a hearty welcome to those who have been away from us and wish them the best of luck in the battles ahead for places in our teams. The Committee has decided that the Club shall return to its full pre-war programme, and a glance at the Fixture List will show that there is a busy season ahead. At the outbreak of war we occupied a position which had never before been attained by any club. We were National Road Walking Champions (20 miles) and English Cross-Country Champions (10 miles). We also won the R.W.A. National "Junior" (qualification basis) Ten Miles' Championship. Our walkers were runners-up in the 50 Kilos Championship, whilst our runners had been placed in the Southern, and the London-Brighton Relay. Of our best Individual Performances, Harry Churcher was our brightest star. A.A.A. Champion at Two and Seven Miles, Inter-Counties Road Walking and Track Champion, unbeaten in Open Road Walks for two seasons. Ted Stimpson and Arthur Penny represented England in the International Cross-Country Race. Tom Carter was Southern Counties' Six Miles Track Champion, he also held the Surrey Title, and was fourth in the A.A.A. Ten Miles' Championship. Eddie Pack was Southern and Inter-Counties 440 yards Champion, and runner-up in the A.A.A. title. Charlie Melchior was second in the Southern and third in the A.A.A. Javelin Throw. Joe Coleman was third in the A.A.A. Seven Miles and third in the Southern Two Miles' Walk. Stan Botwright was third in the Southern Furlong. Many other members gained A.A.A. and Southern Standards, and won honours in County Races. During the war our runners, walkers and field events men have striven hard to uphold the high position held by the Club, and we can say that no other club maintained such a high all-round level of- performance. We can feel justly proud of our war-time record. Now we have to set about the task of defending our titles from teams from all parts of England. We have some very good material for team-building, and the only way to reach championship class is by hard work, regular and systematic training, and a carefully graded racing programme. Our sectional captains will be most pleased to give training advice, etc., to those who need it. Most of our younger members will probably be called up. We sympathise that many will have a promising athletic career interrupted, but, presumably, it will affect all of the same age-group. A number of those already called up have hopes of continuing their athletics with the Forces so that when they come out they will be fit to take on all and sundry. We hope that as many as possible will be able and encouraged to do this, and that all will keep in touch with the Club and visit us when on leave. Meanwhile they have our best wishes and we hope that the support given to us by our serving members during the war will set a tradition of loyalty which they will follow. items.label: November 1945
items.sum: Report of the club's annual general meeting of 13 October 1945, including the election of Percy Wright and Tom Carter to life membership and R. J. Savage's re-election as President.
items.s: THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING Report of the club's annual general meeting of 13 October 1945, including the election of Percy Wright and Tom Carter to life membership and R. J. Savage's re-election as President. This was held at Belgrave Hall on October 13th with the President in the Chair. He opened the meeting by saying that this was the first Annual General Meeting after Victory, and Peace had been won by great sacrifices. Speaking with emotion, he asked the assembly to stand for a few moments in silent memory of the members who had made the supreme sacrifice in order that we might live our lives in freedom. He was pleased that a large number of our members were home and re-united with families and friends. The Hon. Secretary, in introducing his report, said that it had been a difficult year, but the Club's good progress had been maintained. Victory celebrations had interfered with one or two fixtures. He then announced the Committee's decision to revive our pre-war programme. He closed by thanking those many Club Officials who had ungrudgingly given him help during the past year. The Hon. Treasurer then gave us a review of our finances. We had an increase in assets over the previous year. He paid a warm tribute to the continued work of Les Cohen and the Supporters' Club. The sound state of our finances was due to his efforts. The Treasurer expressed his appreciation to the Hon. Auditors, and the accounts were adopted. The Committee's recommendations for Life Membership were then proposed. Percy Wright's abilities as a walker and of his Club spirit, and above all, his great work in the production of the "Belgrave News Letter," were mentioned by his sponsors. Tom Carter's sponsors mentioned his athletic ability, and his good work as a Club Official. The meeting elected these two great sportsmen and clubmen to Life Membership. Alf Harley then addressed a few remarks on behalf of those like himself who have been serving overseas. He expressed a debt of gratitude to all Club Officials who had kept the Club going in difficult times. During the meeting a telegram arrived from Ken O'Kell, wishing us a successful meeting and the best of luck to all Belgravians. Then came the important task of electing Club Officers for the coming year. Mr. R. J. Savage was again elected President. Dick has served us well throughout the last few months, and it would be fitting, said the Hon. Secretary, for him to be in office for our first post-war year. The President thanked the meeting and said that he would do his utmost to keep Belgrave in its present position. The other officials and committee were elected, details can be seen on the inside cover. The name of S. C. Roberts was added to the list of Vice-Presidents. items.label: November 1945
items.sum: Letter from President R. J. Savage thanking members on his re-election, welcoming back returning servicemen and remembering those who died.
items.s: Letter from President R. J. Savage thanking members on his re-election, welcoming back returning servicemen and remembering those who died. Fellow Members, It is very gratifying to me that in recording your appreciation you have elected me as your President for the ensuing year, and I am proud to have this honour once again bestowed upon me. I should like to thank all those who have given me so freely of their valuable time during my first year of office. This help has done so much to ease my task. During the war all these members have held together a club, which they knew, would be appreciated by those whose duties had called them to distant places. A club, so held during such trying times, is, I feel sure, worthy of high places in the Athletic World, and I know that our members will see to this, and make the name of Belgrave honoured, wherever and whenever the occasion arises. Responsible positions that have been held by the club members during the dark years of history, should not go by without special notice. I therefore feel that to all these men, I, on behalf of all members of the club, should thank them, and to say that these duties they have done will not go by unnoticed. To those of you I have been so happy to see once again after being away, I should like to record my pleasure in having you with us. There are still a number of you, I know, anxiously awaiting the time when you can join us; I say to you, may the time be short, and trust that I shall have the great pleasure of welcoming you amongst us once again. There are those who will not come back, those who whilst they were with us we were happy to call our friends, they have laid down their lives. May this big sacrifice not be in vain, and may we all be worthy of their sacrifices, and carry on in such a way that they would have been proud. I send you all my best wishes wherever you may be, and I am confident that we shall all do our best in every way to make this a raal peace-time year. Yours truly, R. J. SAVAGE. R. J. Savage R. J. SAVAGE President

My dearest wish is that I shall be able to continue working for the Club for many years to come. My good wishes are always with the Belgrave and always will be. Very sincerely yours, PERCY WRIGHT. items.label: November 1945
items.sum: Club notes on members' elections to athletics bodies, training arrangements, returned prisoners of war, coaching "schools", recruiting, links with Wirral A.C., St. Gilloise and Birchfield Harriers, and junior successes.
items.s: Club notes on members' elections to athletics bodies, training arrangements, returned prisoners of war, coaching "schools", recruiting, links with Wirral A.C., St. Gilloise and Birchfield Harriers, and junior successes. Congratulations to Alf Harley upon his election to the Chairmanship of the Road Walking Association (Southern Committee). Also to Syd Roberts upon being elected Vice-Chairman. * * * * Dick Savage and Tom Carter have been elected to the Committee of the Surrey County A.A.A. * * * * To cries of "Who is this man?" Harry Shields was recently elected to the Committee of the Southern Counties Cross Country Association. * * * * Belgrave Hall is open for mid-week training on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, from 6.30 p.m. We need hardly stress the need for training with the pack—a factor largely responsible for the success of our teams. * * * * Tooting Track is open for training every Wednesday evening at 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. Bob Jessop and Charlie Cook will be pleased to meet members at Tooting Track on Sunday mornings. * * * * One important reason for the successful working of the Club during the war was that we had a keen, hard-working Committee. We did not hear much about them, but without the individual efforts and team-work of its members, the running of a club like ours would have been impossible. The Committee members often put themselves to great inconvenience to attend meetings, which were held at all sorts of places. Let us be thankful that we had members who, in addition to extra war-time civilian duties, were willing to serve the Club on the administrative side. * * * * Ken Stimpson, brother of our famous Ted, tells us that he met Mr. W. H. Bowers (father of our junior sprinter, killed serving with H.M. Navy). In offering his best wishes to the Club for its continued success, he offered his son's gear to the Club. This gesture, which is much appreciated, will certainly be put to good use. Thank you, Mr. Bowers. * * * * Most things have gone us in price since the war, but the Club Subscription has kept at the same modest figure. The Hon. Treasurer will be pleased to inform members how they stand in this delicate but important matter. We remind members called up for Service that they need pay no subscriptions whilst serving. * * * * We extend a most hearty welcome to our returned Prisoners of War. Alec and Dan Patience are now out of the Army and will be turning up on the Common. Frank Halls reports progress with his leg, Arthur Beales' chief trouble is indigestion. Alf Miller is back at New Malden. We congratulate them on their liberation from the rigour and monotony of captivity, and wish them all a speedy and happy return to normal life, and trust that their worst memories will be soon forgotten and that they will enjoy a well-deserved happiness. * * * * The war, both in Europe and the Far East having been concluded, we shall, as soon as is deemed fit, revert to our pre-war programme of evening meetings and championships. Will all members holding trophies for whatever purposes, kindly advise the Hon. Secretary the particulars of the trophies held? * * * * Once again it will not be out of place to give a word of thanks to Syd Jarlett (Tiny) for his very successful "school" of youngsters whom he looks after at the Tooting Track. None of the great men of the past had volunteered to act as coaches as had been hoped. We are well aware that this means a certain amount of time away from home, but these "schools" need not necessarily be held at Tooting. Arrangements could be made to hold them in a convenient district to suit the coach. For instance, George Clay holds a "school" at New Malden. * * * * Charlie Cook as a recruiting "sergeant" is par excellence. More's the pity he is not younger so that he could take a "school" as in the days of yore. * * * * George Clay has also been very busy recruiting, and he says he has one or two up his sleeve. Ben Lulham, who has helped us once or twice recently, is one of them. * * * * It is interesting to note a new "record" in membership, for with the election of Clifford John, there are now three generations of Redgraves in the Club. Bill, a "back-room boy," his grandad, and a very keen member of the Supporters' Club, Charlie (father), known to most of us as a walker, but also known to a large circle of variety entertainers as the author of "Just a Couple of Pals," and also was recently on the air in the Navy Band Box, and "C.J.," whom we all hope to see in action in about 1965. * * * * Another war-time friendship has been that of Norman Graves and his club, Wirral A.C. We have been favoured on more than one occasion by a visit from a Wirral stalwart, Mr. Evans, and both he and his Hon. Sec., Bill Werton, would like us to pay a visit to Wallasey for a cross-country run. * * * * Les Cohen, always willing to help, despite his exacting job in connection with the Supporters' Club, finds time to promote his firm's annual sports, with the number of competitors running into many hundreds! In his "spare time" he slips up to the City and buys the prizes for our Handicap Meeting in September. No wonder he is thin. * * * * We are sorry to learn that Frank Thomson has been ill again. We all wish him a speedy return to health, so that he can carry on with the good work with the A.A.A. Committee. * * * * Once again we are indebted to Syd Jarlett, George Edrey and Charlie Jones for their help in training. To George Still, our evergreen veteran, for taking the youngsters over the Common on a Saturday afternoon. To all those Officials who have given up their Saturday afternoons to assist as Judges at our Inter-Club and other meetings. I purposely do not mention names, in case anyone is overlooked, but these "backroom boys" know whom I mean. * * * * The famous Brussels club, St. Gilloise, would like us to pay them a visit. What have you to say to that? Their member, Etienne Gailley, joined us during the war period, and Bill Nankerville joined them during his stay in Brussels. Their President would like the bonds of friendship to be a little tighter. * * * * We congratulate Basil Waldon on his winning both the 100 yards and 220 yards Surrey County Juniors Championships at the White City on Whit Monday. He clocked 11.2 for the 100. In the Southern Junior Championships he won his heat in 10.9, and at the end of the season in Club matches at Tooting he was clocked in two separate meetings at 10.7. * * * * Derrick Burfit has been "written up" by more than one athletic writer of repute, as being the most likely of any English runner to beat the elusive 4-minute mile. His convincing win in the Southern Junior Mile in 4.38 at Chiswick and his Middlesex Junior Mile figure of 4.26, show that he is going on the right way. * * * * Extracted from The Stagbearer, the official organ of the Birchfield Harriers: "Our boys are full of praise for the hospitality and welcome extended to them by . . . and to the Belgrave Club and Tom Carter in particular, and have asked me to place on record in this issue their sincere appreciation of all that was done to make the visit so enjoyable, even if it did result in their arriving home with the milk in the morning." I've heard just a little of this "evening out," and just wonder what the wives of Tom and Sir Harry had to say about it! Just as well, perhaps, that "our Bert" was not available! items.h: READ, MARK, LEARN AND INWARDLY DIGEST
items.sum: Cross-country captain C. T. Carter urges members to train hard for the defence of the English Cross-Country title at Leamington Spa on 9 March 1946 and names returning older runners.
items.s: READ, MARK, LEARN AND INWARDLY DIGEST Cross-country captain C. T. Carter urges members to train hard for the defence of the English Cross-Country title at Leamington Spa on 9 March 1946 and names returning older runners. We have now reached a time we have all been waiting for—Cross-Country Championships. Unfortunately some of us will be missing through Service conditions and other reasons beyond our control. Many of us, in fact, I may say most of us, have never experienced a cross-country championship season. If you think you have trained hard, LET ME TELL YOU it is nothing to the way you have got to train if you hope to get in THE Belgrave team which will be called upon to defend its title as English Cross-Country Champions on March 9th, 1946, at Leamington Spa. We were winners of the title when it was last held in 1939. Although six years have elapsed and some of the older members will be returning, I expect to see plenty of fireworks when we all get together again. Members such as Dan, Alec and Ron Patience, Ted Stimpson, Charlie Smart, Jim Ginty, Arthur Penny, Pat Parker, Jimmy Kemp, Bill Lucas and a host of others, not forgetting Bert Footer, the Club's greatest captain of all time. Bert will be the right man to shake you up, which he will no doubt do, having no Commando stuff to mess about with. So you young members, 22 years and upwards, try and show the "old 'uns" how to do it. UP THE BELS. C. T. CARTER, Cross-Country Captain. C. T. Carter C. T. items.label: November 1945
items.sum: News of members serving overseas, including their athletic activities in the Azores, Belgium, Germany, Italy, Africa, India, Burma and Ceylon.
items.s: NEWS OF MEMBERS. News of members serving overseas, including their athletic activities in the Azores, Belgium, Germany, Italy, Africa, India, Burma and Ceylon. As demobilisation proceeds this item will become smaller, but we hope that all members away from home will keep in touch with the Club so that we can give members news of those far away. The Club has in recent years received many letters from members overseas, thanking us for sending them regular (perhaps not too frequent) copies of the Belgravian, and many have expressed particular interest in news of members. So don't forget to let us know where you are, we might be able to give you the address of a member who might be in the next town or village, a thousand miles away! Len Marchant is a regular correspondent from the Azores. He manages to train fairly regularly and won the quarter, half and one mile at a sports meeting. Hopes to be competing at home in the 1946 track season. We all hope to be seeing you too, Len! Is now L.A.C.. He occasionally meets Ray Dunford, who is also in the Azores. Norman Graves. During last cross-country season he took part in many French races, wearing Belgrave Colours. Informs us that the French held their "Nationals" throughout the four years of occupation. Ran second in Wirral A.C. 10 Miles' Championship Cup, when on leave. Will Nankeville has moved to Hamburg from Brussels, where he had a good time with the Union St. Gilloise Club. He ran third to the Belgian champion in the 400 and 800 metres against Royal Racing Club de Brussels. In a 600 metre event he forced the winner to set up a new Belgian record. Later: is now at Belsen. Bert Footer, also somewhere near Hamburg, and training some of his Commandos for a Brigade Race. Frank Elson has been promoting sports in Belgium and won three swimming events and a walking race. Colin Sutton travelled a thousand miles to win a walking race. May be home shortly. Don Brown is now a Chindit and keeping fit. George Durrant writes in admiration of Burmese teak and temples, but not so keen on forcing his way through teak in the jungle from Imphal to Rangoon. Arthur Beaumont reminds us of the ardours of the Italian campaign, and is looking for a change when he returns to civil life. It is rumoured that he was married when on leave recently. Len Rollins writes from Ceylon about perpetual sweating. Is very busy and will be pleased to see any members who happen to be near H.M.S. Bherunda. Jimmy Kemp, with E. Africa Command, and offers us vests and shorts. Has put on weight and "feels the years." Sends congratulations to the lads for their good showing. Frank King enjoyed a welcome leave at home this summer, but had to return to Italy. Bill Snell, very busy in an office job with no P.T. The roads are very bad and over mountains, and it is very hot. Hopes to be home in January. Syd Jones was home on leave during the summer. See Field Events. Bill Sutton was seen at the Hall recently. Jim Heathfield, another one at Hamburg, previously at Bruges. Does no running. Henry Stirling has been in Hong Kong and may be there for another year or so. Len Camin is with S.E.A.C. Bill Hewitt finished second in the 1,500 metres in a district athletic championship at Florence. The winner was an old rival, P. Dee, of Mitcham, who clocked 4.22, with Bill 8 seconds behind. Has met Phillips, of Blackheath. Len Coleman sends his usual cheery letter from W. Africa. Celebrated Victory by burning palm trees and firing spare ammunition into the sea. Won't be home this winter, which, he says, will keep him from the rigours of winter and risk of pneumonia! Ted Stimpson has come up against the famous Midlands International, Reg Draper, in some sports with the B.A.O.R. In the three miles Ted was second in 15.37 against Draper's 15.27, and was second in the one mile in 4.38. His brother is still afloat, and with the Home Fleet. Dick Stride read a recent Belgravian in a foxhole 20 yards from "Jerry." He was second in a Brigade three miles cross-country race, being beaten on the tape in 15.6. In a letter he sent he gave vivid details of house to house fighting in Italy with the London Irish Rifles. Alf Orton is still keeping fit in the desert, and hopes to be at the Hall very soon. Don Abbott is now with the R.A.F. in India. Jack Watts is home again, and sends his regards to his Belgrave and Eastleigh friends. Gordon Harvey is now fit and well in India, and, through his parents, has expressed his continued interest in the Club's activities. Dick Michael has left H.M.S. Sidmouth and is now with H.M.S. Speedy. Charlie Smart is still over the water, and has been winning prizes in France. Obviously very fit! Percy Wilson is still somewhere on the Continent, so brother Joe informs us. Cooper Clark, one time 440 and 880 yards Club Champion, was recently spotted in Vienna by Alf Harley. Cooper is now a corporal in the R.A.F. and sends his best wishes to all his old friends. Len Herbert represented the R.A.F. on many occasions, and won their three miles' championship. Bill Lucas was recently seen wearing the medal ribbon of the Distinguished Flying Cross, also bronze Oak Leaves, denoting "mentioned in despatches." Heartiest congratulations, Bill. Bill flew his total of flying hours in a Wellington bomber during the early days of the war, and made several trips over Germany. Has recently been flying Mosquitoes. He was recently married. Warmest congratulations and best wishes to both. George Long, after five months in Normandy, is back in the mountains of Scotland. David Bayley, one of our newer members, stationed in N. Ireland, ran second in a one mile race over there. The winner was another Belgravian, David Main. Snakey! Is returning to England shortly. Dick Negus is with an officers' training unit in Kent. He injured a knee on an assault course and is to have an operation. Tony Whincup, now at Leicester. Broke sprint records during the fighting in Normandy. Is doing office work. Arthur Cook has been suffering from jaundice. Is expecting release in October, and then back to his megaphone. Norman Shrubb flew home from India to marry Lilian Read, a well-known supporter. They spent their honeymoon walking in Surrey. Best of luck and happiness to you both! Ron Patience was second in the N. Ireland Command three miles' championship. Is probably demobbed by now. Jack Flower is now home and out of the Army. Has put on a lot of weight, a fact readily believed by those who have seen him. Joe Flower writes from Somerset sending best wishes to all of his old friends. Doug. Earle has done no racing for several years, owing to heart-strain. He may be starting again in a mild way. Allan Dunn has been called up to H.M.S. Duke at Malvern. Is keeping fit and has played some rugger. Doug. Woodhead may be doing some cross-country running when the weather is too bad for flying. He used to parachute supplies to resistance movements from Norway to S. France. Frank Webb is now home from S. Africa, but is not yet demobbed from the R.A.F. Dennis Rodaway was recently seen round the S.W.11 district by our old friend Charlie Cook. "Sailor" Johnson recently visited the Hall for a run when on leave. Alan Lomas was at the Hall recently, and is still with the R.A.F. Peter Nunn has been recently called up, and is stationed at Durham. Hopes to keep up running. Albert Boddy has been called up and is with the General Service Corps in Cornwall. Len Spooner has gained another pip and is now a Captain. Congratulations Len! Is expecting an early release. Bert Clayton has been having trouble with his feet and is seeing a specialist. We trust they are soon normal again and that we shall be seeing you on the road soon. Jack Rutland has moved from Wales to Leicester, and recently became the proud father of a son, Graham John. Mention is made elsewhere of his win in the Army Walking Championship. Perhaps what is not generally known is that he completed the last two miles in agony owing to bad blisters—they were wearing boots! That's the stuff champions are made of! Charlie Redgrave nearly went overseas, his age group was called off the boat a few hours before sailing! Has spent a few hours (maybe days) at sea in spite of being at shore establishment. Believes his demob. is not far off. Ken Cuff appeared at the Hall recently wearing a kilt, and seemed even bigger than he did on his last visit. Albert Sampson was a competitor at the Club Handicap meeting after three or more years abroad. He looked very fit. Ray Woodard is to be congratulated upon being elected a Vice-President of Walton A.C. Ray is now a Surgeon-Lieutenant in the Navy, and when living in London was a regular member of George Still's pack. John Brown, who is stationed at Scarborough, gained second place in the Northern Command 880 yard championships. This gained him a place in the N.C. team competing in the Army Championships at Aldershot. He gained fourth place, and as a result was a reserve for the Army team at the White City meeting on August Monday. Percy Wright is another hoping for and expecting an early release. Meanwhile he is still at Newport, but manages frequent visits to town. He was present at the A.G.M. to see the Club show its approval and appreciation of his great services to them by electing him an Hon. Life Member. The B.N.L., now well into its fifth year, is still going strong. It is estimated that he has written over a thousand letters as well as the B.N.L. Harry Churcher hopes to get back to his old form when he is demobbed, which, we learn, is very soon now. It would be grand to see Harry leading them in again, and when we think of pre-war champions who have staged a "come-back," we are very confident. We all wish you the best of luck, Harry. Fred Clay was married this summer and has moved to Leicester. Congratulations and best wishes to you both for your future health and prosperity. Fred hopes to pay us frequent visits. Jock Frost also has our congratulations and best wishes on the occasion of his marriage in August. Don't forget to pass them on to the wife, Jack! Represented the A.A.A. last summer, and won the furlong for them against Northern Counties at Bradford. Fred Rickards, we regret to say, has been invalided from the Police Force. Our sympathies, Fred; we sincerely hope that you will enjoy better health for the change. Arthur Jannaway informs us that he is resting following nervous overstrain. "Jan," since he has taken over the Juniors, has put in some hard work, and we trust that he will soon be with us again, doing the important task of looking after to-morrow's champions. Congrats. on finishing third in the road race at Bexley. Charlie Bond, now living at Barnes, and sends his best wishes to all. Has been signing on new members. Eddie McKeown damaged his shoulders and fingers when playing rugger for Great Britain against N. Ireland last season. Is now fit again, having been selected to play in Paris for his team, Rosslyn Park. Harry Timberlake, although unable to take an active part in sport, is a very willing helper for the Club and for local youth atheltic organisations. Jim Watson was promoted to Inspector early in the year. Congratulations, Jim. Was on sick-leave for a short while, as he strained a few muscles in his neck when rescuing a bomb-victim from a semingly impossible situation. Will Jacques is now recovering from appendicitis at Oakham (Rutland). Will Ellis has had his leg in plaster owing to a torn muscle. Wally Ives is now getting down to civilian life and is back on the trolleybuses again. He is also getting down to it on the road. Arthur Penny is hoping to defend his Ten Miles' Cross-Country title. If Arthur gets really fit, then who ever wishes to win the Macher Shield will have to go all the way. Peter Vine, having recovered from his injury sustained playing football about two years ago, is playing again—this time for Kingstonians. We all wish him the best of luck. Peter Harding's many friends will learn with profoud regret that he has been stricken with infantile paralysis. Peter has our deepest sympathies and ever sincere wishes for a complete and speedy recovery. Alf Harley, Charlie Churcher and Joe Coleman, by virtue of their demobilisations, find themselves in the last part (civilians) of this feature. By the time that these notes appear they will no doubt be playing prominent parts in the Club. Laurie Jackson was at the Club Handicap Meeting, and was still limping. George Tyrer, our oldest cross-country runner, looked in at the Hall recently. Syd King has been out training again; it looks as if we are going to see some old faces in our post-war teams. items.s: BRITISH GAMES. Report on Belgrave members' performances at the British Games at the White City on Whit-Monday, including David Main's Mile win and Derrick Burfitt's Youths' One Mile win. BRITISH GAMES. WHITE CITY (WHIT-MONDAY) Michael Broadbent was inches behind C. B. Holmes in the 100 yards, won in 10.3 secs. In the Youths' Sprint, Basil Walden won his heat in 11.2 secs., qualified in the second round, but was unplaced in the final. Will Nankeville was up the front for most of the way in the 880 yards, but was four yards behind the winner in third place, in 1.59. David Main found his true form in the Mile and won from Nankiwell (Southgate) and Bingham (Finchley) by six yards in 4.37.2. Derrick Burfitt won as he liked in the Youths' One Mile in 4.30. Fred Clay, feeling the effects of a strenuous afternoon the previous Saturday at Dartford, lost his heat in the 100, but won his 220 yards first heat in 24.4, but failed to qualify in the second round. Jack Frost too, had had a strenuous Saturday, having won the furlong for the A.A.A. at Oxford, was unplaced in his heat in the 100 yards, and gave the furlong a miss. Tom Carter was fourth in the Two Miles, won by Doug. Wilson in 9.13.8, Pascoe being third. Stan Botwright tried an unusual distance, the half-mile, but was unplaced. items.s: JUNE 23rd. MATCH v. GILLINGHAM & DISTRICT Report of the 23 June match at Gravesend in which Belgrave and Polytechnic combined against a strong Gillingham & District team, ending in a close result. JUNE 23rd. MATCH v. GILLINGHAM & DISTRICT After the poor show of the previous year we were determined together with Polytechnic, to make amends and prove that we could tackle and beat the best. So, with what must be the strongest team any two clubs in the country could muster, we fought our way through the holiday crowd at Victoria and journeyed to Gravesend to give battle. "What a battle." Jimmy Green had got together a team comprising Cyril Holmes (A.A.A. sprint champion) and notables from all parts of the country. It was unfortunate that a short limit mile was included in the programme, which robbed us of the services of Doug. Wilson, and probably affected the result of the meeting. As it was a close match resulted, and grand performances were put up by our sprinters, Jack Frost and Fred Clay, against such opposition, with Jack Brown, our A.A.A. junior 880 yards champion, others giving their usual sterling performances. A feature of the two miles was the welcome return of Arthur Penny, and we look forward to his return and the assistance he can give in the training of our younger members. Everyone present had a grand afternoon with an excellent tea and dance in the evening to round off a perfect day. items.label: November 1945
items.sum: T. C. Jones's report on Belgrave juniors at the Southern Junior Championships at the Polytechnic Track, Chiswick, on 16 June, where Derrick Burfit retained the Mile title.
items.s: SOUTHERN JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIPS T. C. Jones's report on Belgrave juniors at the Southern Junior Championships at the Polytechnic Track, Chiswick, on 16 June, where Derrick Burfit retained the Mile title. SOUTHERN JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIPS 16th JUNE Southern Junior Championships were again held at the Polytechnic Track at Chiswick this year. The Club's representatives again made their presence felt. In the Mile, Derrick Burfit was defending the title he won last year and after his previous performances it did not look as if there was anyone to extend him. He won his heat in 4 mins. 38.4 secs., and in the final did 4 mins. 38 secs., to record another win. Derrick's ease of running showed the extent of his training and his grasp of the fundamentals of racing technique. He won both heat and final with consummate ease by over 50 yards. Don Adie was the other Belgravian in this race, and whilst he did not reach the final, showed promise. The next event, the 100 yards, was expected to be won by Grieve, but our two representatives were expected to show up well. Basil Walden reached the final and was only beaten by a yard or so to be placed fourth in the fast time of 10.4 secs. Alan Fleming did not get a place in his heat, but with more racing experience, should improve. Bates, our runner in the "Half," showed up very well in his heat to gain second place and reach the final. He was unplaced in this but might possibly have done better if he had gone away with the field at the start instead of making a last quarter effort, which did not avail him much. The final was, however, won in 6 secs. faster time than his heat. In the "Quarter," Heathfield and Freestone were our two runners. Heathfield won his heat in 56.5 secs and although Freestone ran a game race he was unable to get into the placings to enable him to reach the final. Here again, more experience will no doubt enable him to improve. In the final Heathfield put up a very good show, and although only placed fourth, showed that he was not outclassed in a race that was won in 3 secs. faster time than that which won his heat. He told me afterwards that his Army life did not allow him much time for training and this makes his performance all the more creditable. In the field events we had hopes that Alan Dunn would at least be able to reproduce or perhaps improve on his last year's performances and so gain a place in the Javelin. However, his luck seemed to be out, mainly perhaps owing to his not having sufficiently checked his run-up. One throw, given as a "no-throw," was over 180 feet, which would have gained him first place. His actual recorded best throw was just over 145 feet, but he did not gain a place with this. Dennis Fleming, a son of one of our old members, showed promise of bigger things in this event. He is only 16 and with an increase in age and weight, should improve considerably. Alan Fleming, a brother of Dennis, competed in the Long Jump, but had to contend with the long-jumper's bugbear, "No jumps." He, however, showed promise and will no doubt develop in due time. Dunn and Adie also competed in the Discus, Dunn gaining fourth place. T. C. JONES. items.label: November 1945
items.sum: T. C. Jones's review of the season's field events: shot, javelin, discus, high and long jump, promising juniors and a plea for helpers.
items.s: FIELD EVENTS' GOSSIP T. C. Jones's review of the season's field events: shot, javelin, discus, high and long jump, promising juniors and a plea for helpers. FIELD EVENTS' GOSSIP We started off the present season with a serious handicap owing to Jerry Thompson, our best Shot Putter, having been confined to hospital suffering from sugar diabetes. It is to be hoped his recovery will be as speedy as possible, so that we may perhaps be able to have his services in the first post-war season. This loss meant that the brunt of the Shot event fell upon Charlie Melchior. He has gained us useful points in all matches and did a personal best of 34 ft. 8 ins. in the match against the Police at Imber Court. He has been supported by George Weston, one of our veteran runners, on a number of occasions, and also Alan Bishop and Doug. Vine, both of whom are young and should develop into the 35-foot standard soon. Weston has scored successes in the A.A.A. Shot handicaps. In the middle of the season we were glad to see Sid Jones, our Shot Champion, home on leave from Germany. He was persuaded to turn out, and in spite of not being stripped, managed to get second place with an effort of 35 feet 8 ins., showing he has none of his powers impaired. Melchior has also been our leading exponent with the Javelin. Here, again, he has gained us valuable points, in fact, in most matches, we have been able to look upon him as a certain winner. His performances have not been quite as good as in previous seasons. George Powell has once again proved that the passing of the years does not necessarily decrease the powers of the elbow. Alan Dunn, of whom great things were expected this season, did not quite reach the heights expected in the Junior events, but did a wonderful throw of over 160 feet with a senior Javelin in the first of the A.A.A. handicaps, to win. This event has shown a revival in popularity this season, and with more practice and attention to style and technique, Frank Watson, a new member, Bert Machell and our Field Events' Captain, should show some good performances. In the Discus, Charlie Melchior and George Powell have again gained points. We have been glad to welcome a new member in this event in Fred Rowell, who is a Flight Lieutenant in the R.C.A.F. He has proved himself the best of our men and recorded a best performance of 103 ft. 4 ins. Rowell has also been our chief hope in the High Jump. His novel style, not often seen in this country, has enabled him to gain valuable points in matches. Unfortunately Guy Hendry is still in the R.A.F. and has been able to turn out only a few times. In the Club Handicap, however, he did 5 ft. 4 ins., which equalled Rowell's best. Support in this event has been rather lacking and we shall have to unearth some jumpers for next season if we are not to lose too many points in matches. In the Long Jump we have again been unfortunate in not having the services of Tom Wiley, and therefore our Field Events' Captain has been our first string. His best performance was 19 ft. 10½ ins. at Walton. Fred Clay has lent valuable assistance, as have Bert Machell and Alan Fleming. This is another event in which we shall have to unearth some new talent. We have a number of promising Juniors, who next season, it is hoped, will get down to a serious study of the technique of their particular events. Don Adie (Discus and Long Jump), Alan Fleming (Javelin), Drew (Shot), Allen (Shot and Javelin), Freestone (Discus) and George (Long Jump), are names which come to mind. Just one last word. It does not seem to be realised by most people the tremendous amount of work which has to be put into running these events at meetings. The assistance is required of a judge and two marksmen for each event. Added to this it is necessary to run two events together so as to keep pace with the rest of the meeting. Our thanks are due to Neil Crawley, Mr. Morrell, Bill Fleming, Mr. Pollard, Timberlake and others who have assisted in this way during the past season. Don't forget, some of you folk who are just spectators at meetings, if you want to do a job of work, volunteer to do something for the Field Events' men, they will be thankful. Your services can always be utilised. T. C. JONES, Field Events' Captain.
